title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks (Guidance)
author: Evelyn Zhao
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s standards and recommended practices for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and SRE runbooks. It is intended for service owners, SREs, and platform engineers who operate customer-facing inference services (hosted API, Dedicated, Private control plane).

1) SLOs and Error Budgets — Principles and Required Fields

Principles:
- SLOs measure user-visible reliability and are the primary signal for availability decisions.
- Error budgets connect business risk and engineering action: they enable controlled risk-taking (deployments, experiments) while protecting customer experience.
- Every production service must have at least one availability SLO and at least one latency SLO for the primary user path (e.g., token-generation API or model infer call).

Required fields for each SLO entry (service owner must publish in the service doc):
- SLO name (short)
- Service: logical name (e.g., inference-frontend, kvcache-service)
- Owner: team and primary oncall rotation
- Measurement window: rolling 28-day (default) or 7-day for high-change services
- Indicator: success/failure definition (boolean) or latency distribution (pXX)
- Target: numeric target (e.g., 99.9% availability; p95 <= 150ms)
- Data source and query: PromQL/SQL or telemetry path (link to dashboard)
- Error budget burn policy: thresholds and automated actions
- Related alerts and thresholds

SLO Examples (recommended defaults)
- Availability (hosted inference API): Indicator = request success (2xx, or well-formed error that still meets SLA). Window = 28d. Target = 99.95%.
- Tail latency (model inference path): Indicator = request latency. Window = 28d. Target = p95 <= 120ms (for small models) or p95 <= 300ms (for long-seq / large-model variants).
- Embeddings throughput success: Target = 99.9% within throughput quota windows.

SLO Table (example)
Service | Indicator | Window | Target | Owner | Data source
------ | --------- | ------ | ------ | ----- | -----------
inference-api | availability (2xx) | 28d | 99.95% | eng-infra-oncall | grafana:/dashboards/inference-api-availability
model-runtime | latency (p95) | 28d | 120ms | serving-runtime | metrics:/model-runtime/p95

Error Budget Burn Policy (standard)
- Green: remaining budget > 90% — normal operations and deploys allowed.
- Yellow: remaining budget 60%–90% — restrict high-risk deploys, require one approver from SRE. Increase monitoring and post-deploy checks.
- Orange: remaining budget 30%–60% — pause non-essential experiments, require staged rollout and SRE oversight.
- Red: remaining budget < 30% — roll back risky changes, prioritize remediation tickets, schedule a war room if burn risk persists for >12 hours.

Automated responses (examples)
- If availability error budget burn rate > 5x baseline for 1 hour, trigger a high-severity PagerDuty notification to service owner and SRE lead.
- If latency error budget declines past yellow for two consecutive days, open a P1 action item and schedule focused triage (see Incident Review Standards).

2) Capacity Planning — Process and Templates

Goals:
- Ensure capacity meets SLOs across traffic patterns (diurnal, burst, tail events).
- Provide procedures for provisioning Dedicated pools and autoscaling behavior.

Quarterly capacity planning workflow (owner: eng-sre + service owner)
1. Data collection (weeks -3 to -2):
   - Export 90/95/99 percentile request rates, sequence length distribution, and model-mix from telemetry for past 90 days.
   - Collect business forecasts (sales, marketing campaigns, onboarding) from product.
2. Model & configuration review (week -2):
   - Determine dominant model families (quantized vs fp16), expected memory/kv-cache requirements, and batching opportunities.
3. Headroom calculation (week -2):
   - Use standard headroom formula: required_capacity = peak_qps * p99_latency_headroom_factor * safety_margin. Document parameters used.
4. Procurement & reservation (week -1):
   - Submit Dedicated capacity requests to cloud procurement or on-prem capacity team.
5. Validation & runbook updates (week 0):
   - Execute soak tests and chaos experiments (small scale) to validate autoscaling and circuit-breakers. Update runbooks with any new mitigation steps.

Autoscaling policy guidelines
- For inference-frontend: target CPU/GPU utilization = 60% average over 5m, scale step = 1 unit, cooldown = 5m.
- For model-runtime pools: scale based on queue length and token-in-flight metric instead of raw GPU utilization for steady tail-latency control.
- Prefer horizontal scaling with smaller instances over large monoliths to reduce tail-latency impact.

Capacity table (example parameters)
Service | Metric | Scale trigger | Target utilization
------- | ------ | ------------- | ------------------
inference-frontend | RPS | > 70% of capacity for 3m | 60%
model-runtime-small | tokens-in-flight | queue_length > 100 | 55%

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

Runbook of common reliability projects (owner: reliability-initiatives squad)
- Automatic KV-prefix caching (Q2): reduce per-token compute by 12% for repeated prefix workloads. Metrics: cache hit rate, impact on latency p95.
- Router intelligent fallbacks (Q3): route to compatible model variant when primary pool is saturated. Metrics: % requests auto-failed-over, customer impact index.
- Observability Uplift (ongoing): instrument token-level traces and end-to-end latency histograms for all critical paths.

Prioritization criteria
1. SLO impact (failure mode severity and frequency)
2. Cost efficiency (expected cost reduction per unit of engineering effort)
3. Customer impact (enterprise customers affected, SLAs)
4. Operational complexity (runbook length, human toil)

4) Incident Review Standards (Postmortems and RCA)

Purpose: produce blameless, well-scoped postmortems that capture root causes, impact, timeline, and corrective actions.

Postmortem template (required fields)
- Title
- Severity (P1/P2/P3)
- Incident window (start, detection, mitigation, resolution)
- Impact summary (customer-visible effects, affected routes, error budget impact)
- Timeline of key events (timestamped)
- Root cause analysis (technical cause + contributing factors)
- Corrective actions (short-term mitigation, medium-term fix, long-term prevention)
- Owner for each action and due date
- Detection and monitoring improvements (metric and alert changes)
- Learnings and follow-ups (team-level retro items)

Incident review cadence
- P1 incidents: postmortem required within 72 hours, full RCA published within 7 days.
- P2 incidents: postmortem required within 7 days.
- Review meeting: weekly incident-review board reviews new postmortems and verifies action closure.

Templates for RCA techniques
- 5 Whys (useful for process-driven failures)
- Fault tree analysis (for complex multi-system outages)
- Heap/trace correlation (for runtime issues)

5) Operational Tooling — Dashboards, Alerts, and Automation

Standard dashboards (owned by eng-sre)
- SLO Overview: single-pane showing availability and latency SLOs across top services.
- Token-level cost and latency drilldown: per-model, per-route.
- Capacity & utilization: GPU/CPU pools, queue length heatmaps.
- Error taxonomy: grouped by error code, model variant, and region.

Alerting standards (alert fatigue reduction)
- Alert = actionable & specific. Each alert must include: symptom, runbook link, owner rotation.
- Severity mapping: P0/P1 for immediate paging alerts, P2 for high-signal email/SMS, P3 for dashboards only.
- Use alert deduplication and suppression windows for cascading failures.

Recommended automation
- Auto-escalation when error-budget burn crosses red for >1h.
- Runbook-driven remediation playbooks (infra-as-code runbooks) that can perform safe rollback or scale up by policy.
- Canary analysis automation: run automated canary checks post-deploy and block rollout on regressions.

6) SRE Runbooks — Format and Examples

Runbook format (required)
- Title
- Scope & impact (what system, what user-visible effects)
- Symptoms (how it's detected)
- Immediate actions (1–5 steps)
- Diagnostics (commands and dashboards)
- Mitigation (short-term fixes)
- Remediation (long-term fix steps)
- Owner & escalation path
- Post-incident actions (what to update after resolution)

Example runbook: High tail latency on model-runtime
- Scope: model-runtime pools serving transformer models; affects p95 and p99 latency for inference API.
- Symptoms: p95 > baseline by 2x for >5m, increase in queuing tokens-in-flight and GPU p95 latency.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Notify oncall and open incident channel.
  2. Reduce new request load by enabling rate-limiter policy for non-enterprise routes.
  3. Add additional model-runtime instances (scale out min by 2) via infra tooling.
  4. If queue length continues rising, failover critical routes to backup region/model-variant.
- Diagnostics commands:
  - kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=model-runtime -o wide
  - metrics query: sum(rate(tokens_in_flight[5m])) by (pool)
  - trace example: open jaeger / traces?service=model-runtime&span=generate
- Mitigation: temporarily route long-seq requests to dedicated long-seq pool; adjust batching windows.
- Remediation: identify root cause (e.g., memory leak, kernel regression, model OOM) and create two follow-up tickets: immediate patch + post-deploy soak.

Example runbook: Capacity exhaustion for Dedicated pool
- Symptoms: autoscaling fails to provision new nodes; queue grows; customers see 429 or degraded latency.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Trigger manual provisioning of reserved capacity from Dedicated control plane.
  2. Activate overflow routing to hosted pool (if contract allows) or communicate with account team for temporary quota increase.
  3. Roll back recent configuration changes that increased per-request cost (if applicable).
- Diagnostics: check cloud quota, spot instance reclaim logs, and autoscaler events.

7) Ownership, Oncall, and Runbook Maintenance

- Each service must designate an SLO owner and a runbook owner. Runbook owner is responsible for ensuring runbook accuracy after each incident.
- Oncall rotations should be documented in the runbook header with links to PagerDuty schedules.
- Runbook review cycle: minor updates — quarterly; major changes — after any P1 (within 14 days).

8) Rollouts, Canarying, and Experimentation Policy

- Canary scale: initial canary = 2% traffic, validate metrics (SLOs, error rate, resource utilization) for 30 minutes before increasing to 10%.
- Experiments that impact >5% traffic require SRE approval and documented rollback plan.
- Progressive rollouts for model changes: small-model -> mid-model -> large-model pools, with automated monitoring gates.

9) Metrics, Dashboards, and Signals to Track

Minimum signal set for service owners
- Availability (success rate), Latency (p50/p95/p99), Error budget remaining (28d), Request rate (RPS/qps), Queue length / tokens-in-flight, GPU utilization, OOM/eviction counts, Cache hit rate.

10) Related Pages and References

- See also: confluence/eng-sre/sre-slos-capacity-and-runbooks-2025.json
- Reference: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture (model runtime instrumentation)
- PagerDuty playbook: confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process

Appendix: Useful queries and CLI snippets
- Example PromQL (p95 latency):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- Example query for availability (28d):
  1 - sum(rate(http_requests_total{code!~"2.."}[28d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[28d]))

Document maintenance
- Owner: Evelyn Zhao (eng-sre)
- Review cadence: annual full review, quarterly spot-checks.

Questions or updates: ping #eng-sre on Slack or email eng-sre@redwood.ai for urgent updates.
